newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: De Beers mulls multiple Russian suppliers.
newsitem.headline: De Beers mulls multiple Russian suppliers.

text.p: De Beers said on Wednesday its decision to abandon its current Russian diamond sales pact would leave it free to negotiate favourable terms of sale with individual suppliers within that country.

De Beers said earlier on Wednesday it will stop buying Russian diamonds from December 31 under the terms of this agreement. It, however, added that it expected to continue buying significant amounts of Russian stones.

"After January 1, 1997 we will obviously be free to negotiate with any Russian authority to protect our commercial interests," Gary Ralfe managing director of De Beers' Central Selling Organisation said.

"We will be free...to buy Russian diamonds on the basis that we and them can agree -- a willing buyer, willing seller arrangement without any obligation on our side as we did under the old agreement," he said, addressing analysts and the media.
Under the old agreement, which officially expired at the end of last year, but remained operational as long as no new pact was agreed, De Beers did business with only two authorities.

Ralfe said De Beers had not yet entered negotiations with any new parties. But the absence of an agreement gave De Beers greater flexibility as before it could obviously not buy Russian gems on offer on the international market.
"It will also leave us free to intervene in the diamond markets of Antwerp, Tel Aviv and elsewhere in a way that hitherto we have felt inhibited to," Ralfe said.

The South African company has been in protracted talks with Russia to reach a new agreement to market the country's rough diamonds through the CSO. Although an agreement was reached with ARS in September, approval from the Russian government is still outstanding.
Ralfe said interim arrangements had not worked, with a a large quantity of Russia gems leaking onto the international market.
"In addition to goods out of the stockpile we have also seen current production leaking out," he said.
Ralfe said Russia in the second half of the year had not, as in the first six months, delivered its full diamond entitlement to the CSO.
"They have delivered less than what they were entitled to deliver in respect of 1996," Ralfe said.
